claims.text: A tungsten–vanadium–niobium-based refractory high-entropy alloy can serve as a low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
The proposed alloy combines tungsten's high melting point with reduced nuclear activation from vanadium and niobium.
Tungsten possesses irradiation resistance suitable for the proposed application.
The initial refractory HEA is a homogenized, single-phase solid solution containing multiple refractory elements.
Conventional melting and thermomechanical treatments can optimize the microstructure of a tungsten–vanadium–niobium-based refractory HEA.
The processed alloy will have a uniform elemental distribution.
The processed alloy will maintain a stable grain-boundary structure during high-temperature exposure and irradiation.
The high-entropy effect stabilizes the alloy's solid solution.
The high-entropy effect retards phase separation and precipitation in the alloy.
Vanadium and niobium do not produce long-lived radioactive isotopes under fast-neutron bombardment.
Combining tungsten with vanadium and niobium enables the alloy to withstand high thermal loads and irradiation without excessive activation.
Under fusion-reactor-like thermal and irradiation conditions, the alloy will retain superior high-temperature strength.
Under fusion-reactor-like conditions, the alloy will exhibit excellent irradiation resistance.
The alloy will produce fewer long-lived activation products than conventional plasma-facing materials.
Conventional tungsten components suffer from high activation levels.
Reduced-activation ferritic/martensitic steels have lower high-temperature performance than the proposed refractory HEA.
Plasma-facing-component operating temperatures can be significantly higher than conventional steels can sustain.
